voiceover.text: Here's the chain from last time, with an empty fuel line beside it. Most of us have eaten too soon before training and regretted it: heavy, sick, a stitch. But the food hasn't changed. So what has changed? And why can you feel the same thing before a big race, having eaten nothing unusual?

Fuel starts in one long tube, with helpers alongside. Digestion is mechanical, breaking food into pieces, and chemical, using enzymes to split the molecules. The oesophagus pushes food down by waves of muscle, called peristalsis. The stomach churns it with acid, then releases it slowly. The small intestine does most digestion and almost all absorption, across millions of villi: a huge folded surface with thin walls and blood close by, like the alveoli. The large intestine takes back water. The liver makes bile and stores glycogen, the gallbladder releases bile to split fat into droplets, and the pancreas adds enzymes.

Carbohydrate becomes glucose, carried in the blood or stored as glycogen in muscle and liver, the main fuel at moderate and high intensity. Protein becomes amino acids, mostly to build and repair muscle, and only a small share of fuel. Fat becomes fatty acids and glycerol, the main fuel at rest and low intensity. It packs about thirty-seven kilojoules a gram, against seventeen for carbohydrate, but releases energy slowly, and only with oxygen. That's why running out of glycogen can end a race, while the runner still carries plenty of fat.

Vitamins and minerals, the micronutrients, supply no energy at all, but they make energy usable. Iron builds haemoglobin. Calcium builds bone and triggers muscle contraction, and vitamin D lets you absorb it. B vitamins run the reactions that release energy from food. Sodium and potassium keep fluid balanced and let nerves and muscles fire, and sweat takes them away. So macronutrients supply the fuel and building materials. Micronutrients let the body use them.

Now control. The endocrine system is a set of glands that release hormones into the blood. A hormone reaches every cell, but only acts on cells with a matching receptor. Compare nerves. They send electrical signals to one target in milliseconds. Hormones take seconds to hours, reach anywhere, and last minutes to days. The hypothalamus and pituitary are the control centre, releasing growth hormone. The adrenal glands release adrenaline and cortisol. And the pancreas releases insulin and glucagon.

scenes.title: the pancreas, and the glucose thermostat

voiceover.text: So the pancreas belongs to both systems. It digests carbohydrate into glucose, then releases the hormones that decide what happens to that glucose: supply and control in one organ. After a meal, blood glucose rises, so the pancreas releases insulin, which moves glucose into cells. Glucose falls, and insulin stops. When glucose drops too low, glucagon releases more from liver glycogen. That's negative feedback: a change triggers a response that reverses it, like a thermostat.

Follow one training session. Before and at the start, adrenaline raises heart rate, releases glucose, and opens the taps to muscle while closing those to the gut. So a meal still in your stomach is digested much more slowly, and that's why you feel sick. During the session, glucagon holds blood glucose steady as muscles use it, and in long sessions cortisol frees fat for fuel. As you sweat, antidiuretic hormone, from the pituitary, holds onto water, and aldosterone, from the adrenal glands, holds onto salt. Afterwards, when you eat, insulin refills glycogen, and growth hormone repairs tissue, mostly in deep sleep. That's why sleep is part of training.

That answers the race question too. Nerves before a race release the same adrenaline, pulling blood from the gut. That's acute stress, and it's useful, because it gets you ready to move. The problem is chronic stress, the kind that doesn't switch off. Then the gut's movement and blood flow stay upset for weeks, causing nausea and cramps. And cortisol stays high, keeping the body breaking down when it should be rebuilding. Muscle protein breaks down, recovery slows, illness comes more often, and sleep suffers, which cuts growth hormone. Poor sleep raises stress again, so the loop feeds itself.

Other factors work the same way. Fat, fibre and protein slow the stomach, so pre-training meals are light, mostly carbohydrate. Dehydration slows absorption, just when you need fluid most. Poor sleep cuts growth hormone and raises cortisol. The serious one is low energy availability: eating less than training needs. The body quietly cuts spending on hormones, bone and immunity, so it shows up as stress fractures and repeated illness. Weight loss isn't a good sign here. It's a reason to see a doctor.
Two things to remember. Digestion supplies, hormones control, and the pancreas does both. And acute stress prepares you, but chronic stress wears you down.
Two exam questions. First. Explain how stress impacts on the efficiency of the digestive and endocrine systems. Pause here to answer.

Start with acute stress as useful: adrenaline releases fuel and sends blood from the gut to the muscles. Then the same responses, sustained, become harmful. Less gut blood slows digestion and causes nausea, and high cortisol breaks down muscle, slows recovery, weakens immunity and disturbs sleep. The classic mistake is treating all stress as harmful.

scenes.title: attempt two (the rower in the heat)

voiceover.text: Second. A rower trains for ninety minutes in the heat without drinking. Explain how two hormones help her body hold on to water and sodium, and why she still needs to drink. Pause here to answer.

Sweat lowers body water, so the pituitary releases antidiuretic hormone, and the kidneys keep water. Sodium is lost too, so the adrenal glands release aldosterone, and the kidneys keep sodium. Both are negative feedback, cutting further losses. But hormones can't replace what's already gone, so she must drink. The classic mistake is saying the hormones replace the lost water.

So, for any factor, ask what it does to supply, and to control. Now picture the session's hormones on one timeline, acting over seconds to hours. But catching a ball takes a fraction of a second. Something much faster must be in charge.
